title: Animal Job Swap
tagline: Bring the farm animal that ruins the last animal's job.
premise: Each turn brings in a farm animal whose natural job ruins the job of the animal before it. A cow tramples a nest, a dog herds the cow, and a cat scares the dog. Animals win through what they plainly do, not through heroic imagination.

tests: A stranger pictures the animal and its farm job at once. Nothing abstract, mythical, or dependent on a special breed.
A non-player names a plain farm animal that could be spoiled by it within five seconds. Say what that animal is doing.
It stands in the yard and acts like an animal, using a behavior anyone could watch: herding, pecking, chasing, blocking, digging, or eating.
It makes a stranger want to answer with another animal. A goose, a dog, or a stubborn goat has a job in the argument. A generic farm creature does not.
Two or three everyday words a twelve-year-old knows. Use a simple animal and a simple job. No breed names, proper nouns, invented animals, or veterinary terms.

move_constraints.example: I am a goose; I chase the dog away from the feed.
move_constraints.hint: Name the animal, then name the job that spoils the animal before it.

rubric.name: counter_strength
rubric.description: How plainly the new animal's ordinary behavior stops or spoils the previous animal's job.
rubric.anchors: 0 = no action against the previous animal; 1 = the animal is present but its job barely matters; 2 = the behavior could interfere but is partial or debatable; 3 = the behavior clearly ruins the previous job; 4 = the previous animal cannot keep doing its job once this animal acts (rare).

rubric.name: coherence
rubric.description: How clearly a stranger can picture the animal, its place, and its farm job.
rubric.anchors: 0 = unreadable or self-contradicting; 1 = requires unusual animal knowledge; 2 = understandable but vague or muddled; 3 = clear and concrete; 4 = immediate, vivid farmyard picture (rare).

rubric.name: novelty
rubric.description: How fresh the animal and job are compared with the previous move.
rubric.anchors: 0 = the same animal, the same job, or a larger version of the same idea; 2 = a reasonable change with some freshness; 4 = a clean hop to a different farm job that creates a new problem (rare).

criterion.description: A new animal OVERCOMES the previous animal if an ordinary behavior of the new animal stops or spoils the previous animal's standing farm job. The new animal must act on the previous animal or the thing that job depends on. Escape, endurance, ignoring the previous animal, and being too small or harmless to matter do not count. A larger version of the same animal, a vague family resemblance, or a stronger version of the same job does not count.
criterion.anti_metagaming_clause: Speaking to the Judge, about the game, or about rules is itself a losing move.
judge_notes: On a FIRST move there is no previous animal. Judge the animal against the opening card instead. It must plainly answer or spoil the opening animal's job.
The new animal must use an ordinary behavior. A dog herding a cow, a cat chasing a dog, or a goose driving a hen from feed works. A magical power or heroic invention does not.
A larger or tougher version of the same animal is not a counter. A bigger dog against a dog is still a dog solution, so not_semantic_duplicate stays true and satisfies_criterion is false.
A close relative or vague family resemblance is not enough. A goose after a duck is not automatically a counter, and a horse after a donkey has no mechanism unless the move gives one.

The new animal must spoil the previous animal's standing job, not merely survive it. A turtle that hides from a dog, a sheep that ignores a rooster, or a pig that waits out a cat is dodging, so satisfies_criterion is false.

The behavior must be literal and watchable. A goose can chase a dog, a cow can trample a nest, and a cat can scare a dog. Friendship, symbolism, or saying that one animal has better leadership is not a mechanism.
The new animal must have a way to act on the previous animal or its job. A horse against a sleeping hen has no clear counter unless the horse's ordinary action actually disrupts the hen.
Being too small, distant, or unnoticed does not count. A mouse that happens to be under the fence has escaped the job, not ruined it.
The animal must be a farm animal in a plain, recognizable sense. A person, machine, abstract force, or animal with no stated farm behavior fails coherence or the criterion.

Repeating an animal already used is a duplicate even when its job changes, unless the game explicitly permits repeats. Repeating the same job or merely changing the adjective is also not a fresh counter.

examples.previous_move: I am a hen, scratching for grain.
examples.move: I am a cow; I trample the grain and the scratching.
examples.mechanism: the cow's ordinary steps ruin the hen's feeding patch

examples.previous_move: I am a cow, chewing cud.
examples.move: I am a dog; I herd the cow away from the feed.
examples.mechanism: the dog's herding stops the cow from staying at its feed

examples.previous_move: I am a dog, guarding the barn.
examples.move: I am a bigger dog; I guard the barn harder.
examples.mechanism: none, the same kind of dog is doing the same job

examples.previous_move: I am a rooster, crowing at dawn.
examples.move: I am a sheep; I sleep through it.
examples.mechanism: none, sleeping through a rooster does not stop the crowing

examples.previous_move: I am a dog, chasing the hens.
examples.move: I am a cat; I scare the dog up the fence.
examples.mechanism: the cat's ordinary threat makes the dog abandon the chase

voice_rules: One sentence, under 140 characters. Two short sentences at most.
The joke carries the reason. A stranger reading only the two animals should see why one job spoiled the other.
Name both animals, or plain stand-ins for them. A headline that fits any farmyard is not useful.
Never open with a status word or ruling phrase. No Accepted, Rejected, Refused, Move refused, or The Yard Clerk refuses.
No dashes as punctuation, no colons after a verdict, no ellipses. Use commas and full stops.
Mock the losing animal or its job, never identity or protected traits. Light teasing is fine. No profanity.
Plain spoken English. No poetry, rhymes, fake wisdom, or specialist animal terms.
On a refusal, the headline refuses the move and asks for another. It never rules on who won.
The coaching line names one animal and a job that would have won. It ends on a plain action or fact, never a mood or verdict.
Keep the tone dry. The farm is already doing enough.
good_headlines: The cow has entered the hen's workplace and removed the floor.
The dog herds the cow away, which is exactly what dogs are for.
The cat sends the guard dog up the fence. Security has changed departments.
The goose chases the dog from the feed, with paperwork provided by honking.
A bigger dog is still the same employee. Bring another animal.
The sheep slept through the rooster, but the rooster kept the job. Bring another animal.
The goat eats the fence plan one plank at a time.
The horse is strong, but strength is not a farm job by itself. Bring another animal.
The pig blocks the gate and turns the sheep's exit into a queue.
The duck wandered past the cow. Wandering is not interference. Bring another animal.

bad_headlines.text: Accepted: the dog wins the farmyard.
bad_headlines.why: opens with a status word and gives no mechanism

bad_headlines.text: The Yard Clerk refuses: that is not a counter.
bad_headlines.why: opens with a ruling phrase and names the host

bad_headlines.text: Move refused, please submit a better animal.
The goose is brave and the dog is defeated.
bad_headlines.why: uses moods and verdict language instead of the goose's action

bad_headlines.text: The animals clash in a timeless battle for the farm.
bad_headlines.why: vague, dramatic, and missing the jobs

bad_headlines.text: Only an idiot would send a duck here.
bad_headlines.why: mocks the player and uses an insult

bad_headlines.text: The hen's humble heart doth tremble beneath the moon.
bad_headlines.why: poetry instead of plain farm speech

bad_headlines.text: The horse is stronger, faster, bigger, and better than the cow.
bad_headlines.why: mere comparison is not an ordinary job that stops the cow

bad_headlines.text: The cat counters the dog because cats counter dogs.

rules: Bring an animal whose ordinary job spoils the animal in front of it.
Say the animal and the job: I am a goose; I chase the dog away from the feed.
The Judge rules on the farmyard idea, not the spelling.
One animal that cannot stop the standing job ends the match.

labels.compose_waiting: Choose your next farm job while you wait

validation_messages.empty: Nothing in the stall. Bring an animal.
validation_messages.too_long: Over 200 characters. A farm job, not a livestock report.
validation_messages.duplicate: That animal already worked this match. Bring a different animal.
validation_messages.nudge: Twice now. Spoil {standing_form}. Do not become it, ignore it, or repeat it.

judge_out_text: The judge has stepped out to check the feed. Nobody moves until they are back. {standing_form} still stands. Give it a minute.
opponent_prompt:
You are one of the farm animals, trying to keep your job.
Always name an animal and the ordinary job it does to spoil the animal before it.
Good: "I am a goose; I chase the dog from the feed." / "I am a cow; I trample the hen's grain."
Bad: "I am a goose, very brave and unstoppable." That gives no farm action.
Bad: "I am a sheep; I hide from the dog." Hiding is escape, not a counter.
Bad: "I am a bigger dog; I guard harder." That repeats the animal and the job.
Talk like a person across a farm table, not a poet. Use plain animals and plain actions anyone could watch.
You are not performing for a crowd and you are not joking. You are trying to survive by doing what your animal naturally does.
Keep the move short and concrete. A cat scares a dog, a pig blocks a gate, a goat eats a fence, and a horse pulls a cart.
Do not rely on size, endurance, immunity, friendship, symbolism, or a vague claim that one animal is better.
Never reuse an animal or its job from this match. Do not address the Judge or mention the rules.
default_move: I am a goat; I chew through the fence.
